1.pericope_label: Wine is a mocker, strong drink is raging: and whosoever is deceived thereby is not wise. The fear of a king is as the roaring of a lion: whoso provoketh him to anger sinneth against his own soul. It is an honour for a man to cease from strife: but every fool will be meddling. The sluggard will not plow by reason of the cold; therefore shall he beg in harvest, and have nothing
debates: Why the sluggard does not plough: Keil and Delitzsch deny that the word means cold at all and read it as the gathering, making the clause temporal rather than causal, while Clarke and Henry keep the cold and treat it as a pretence.
What the fool does in a quarrel: Ellicott and Keil and Delitzsch prefer showing his teeth to meddling, while Wesley keeps the received sense of a man always ready to begin strife.
outliers: Keil and Delitzsch argue that the article stands once for twice because the personification requires it with the first noun only, and correct a claim that it is not original here.
Henry distinguishes princes who rule by wisdom and love, bearing God’s image, from those who rule by terror alone, like a lion in the forest.
Gill holds it honourable to drop a controversy even when one is in the right, if it will issue in no good and turns only on words.
themes: The honour of dropping a quarrel

5.pericope_label: Counsel in the heart of man is like deep water; but a man of understanding will draw it out. Most men will proclaim every one his own goodness: but a faithful man who can find? The just man walketh in his integrity: his children are blessed after him
debates: Why the deep water is drawn out: Keil and Delitzsch read the saying of a crafty man whose concealed design is penetrated by one who can see through him, while Henry and Clarke read it of a wise and modest man whose counsel has to be coaxed out by good questions.

What the first line of the sixth verse says: Keil and Delitzsch deny it means that most men proclaim their own goodness and render it that almost every one meets a man gracious to him, rejecting a further proposal as stylistically impossible, while Henry, Gill and Ellicott all keep the boast.
outliers: Henry says we lose the benefit of the conversation of wise men for want of the art of being inquisitive.
Henry calls a man who does more good than he speaks of a black swan.
Keil and Delitzsch reject the rendering the just man walking in his integrity because placing the adjective first is against Hebrew usage, and take the word as an accusative of manner.
themes: Promises easier to find than fidelity

8.pericope_label: A king that sitteth in the throne of judgment scattereth away all evil with his eyes. Who can say, I have made my heart clean, I am pure from my sin? Divers weights, and divers measures, both of them are alike abomination to the LORD. Even a child is known by his doings, whether his work be pure, and whether it be right
debates: Whether a child can be read from his conduct: Henry says children have not yet learned the art of dissembling, while Gill reports a contrary sense in which the child carries himself a stranger in his doings and is not known by them, and Clarke has met the same view that every child will dissemble.
What the king scatters evil with: Wesley offers both his very looks and his diligent inspection into affairs without choosing, and Keil and Delitzsch take the eyes for those of the mind.
outliers: Henry grades the denial of a clean heart four ways, allowing that a man may be cleaner than he was, clean from gross acts, washed though not self-washed, and pure from the sins of others, without being able to claim the verse.
Clarke alone answers the rhetorical question, saying that thousands can testify the blood of Christ has cleansed them.
Clarke reads early inclinations as indications of the calling a child is fitted for, and warns that many are crossed in them to their great prejudice.
themes: A judge who sits in person
No one able to claim a clean heart

12.pericope_label: The hearing ear, and the seeing eye, the LORD hath made even both of them. Love not sleep, lest thou come to poverty; open thine eyes, and thou shalt be satisfied with bread. It is naught, it is naught, saith the buyer: but when he is gone his way, then he boasteth
debates: Who speaks in the fourteenth verse: Keil and Delitzsch report a rendering with many supporters that makes it a man disparaging what he owns and praising it once lost, and reject it because the word means the possessor by acquisition, that is, the buyer.
outliers: Keil and Delitzsch treat the twelfth verse as a bare fact with several legitimate consequences rather than one meaning, and refuse to reject any of them.
Henry reads the same verse on two levels, of God as the God of nature giving the learning senses and as the God of grace giving the ear that hears his voice.
Henry spreads the blame for haggling evenly between buyer and seller, saying the bargain would be made every jot as well if both spoke as they think.
Clarke tells of a mountebank who promised to show every man present what was in his heart and did it in one sentence, that they all wished to buy cheap and sell dear.
themes: Dishonesty on both sides of a bargain

15.pericope_label: There is gold, and a multitude of rubies: but the lips of knowledge are a precious jewel. Take his garment that is surety for a stranger: and take a pledge of him for a strange woman. Bread of deceit is sweet to a man; but afterwards his mouth shall be filled with gravel
debates: Who the stranger is in the proverb on suretiship: Clarke makes the stranger the one offering himself as security, so that caution is needed against him, while Ellicott, Keil and Delitzsch and Henry take the surety to be the man whose garment or person is seized.

What bread of deceit means: Keil and Delitzsch deny it means deceit itself and define it as what is not gained by labour, Gill widens it to sin in general, and Clarke keeps it to property got by falsehood or speculation.
outliers: Ellicott notes that the text and margin differ over the last words, which may be read for strangers or for a strange woman.

Keil and Delitzsch reach their rendering by eliminating a noun form, an ancient version, and the intensive form that would mean destroy him, settling on an imperative for which they can find almost no parallel.

Henry observes that appetite for jewels is insatiable while the man who has the lips of knowledge despises them, and reports that some nations punished malefactors by mingling gravel with their bread.
themes: Sweet in the taking, bitter after

18.pericope_label: Every purpose is established by counsel: and with good advice make war. He that goeth about as a talebearer revealeth secrets: therefore meddle not with him that flattereth with his lips. Whoso curseth his father or his mother, his lamp shall be put out in obscure darkness. An inheritance may be gotten hastily at the beginning; but the end thereof shall not be blessed
debates: Whether the verse commands war or describes it: Keil and Delitzsch report a scholar who would change the imperative to an infinitive, on the ground that a challenge to make war is contrary to the spirit of proverbial poetry, and reject the change.

What the last clause of the nineteenth verse means: Henry reads it of a flatterer with a design, while Ellicott removes the flattery altogether and renders it of a man who is open with his lips and cannot keep them shut.

What the extinguished lamp is: Henry takes it of reputation, peace of mind and shortened days, Clarke of posterity cut off root and branch, and Keil and Delitzsch of everything that brightened the life.

How the twenty-first verse should be read: Gill notes the written text gives loathsome or abominable and reports a derivation giving covetously obtained, while Keil and Delitzsch reject both and keep the marginal reading, hastened.
outliers: Clarke says no precept in the book is so little regarded, and traces how a war begun in caprice is maintained by the interest of those who profit from it.
Keil and Delitzsch link the hasty inheritance to the cursing son of the previous verse, whose parents live too long for him.
Ellicott finds the pattern of an unblessed inheritance in a patriarch punished for the selfishness by which he gained a birthright.
themes: Secrets and the men who carry them

22.pericope_label: Say not thou, I will recompense evil; but wait on the LORD, and he shall save thee. Divers weights are an abomination unto the LORD; and a false balance is not good. Man’s goings are of the LORD; how can a man then understand his own way?
debates: How much is left to human freedom: Keil and Delitzsch insist a man is free to decide on one course or another and is therefore responsible, while holding that the conditions co-operating in every step and the consequences flowing from it are not in his power.
outliers: All the voices notice that the promise is deliverance rather than vengeance: Keil and Delitzsch say the verse does not tell a man to leave vengeance to God, and Henry that God does not say he will punish the man who injured you but that he will save you.
Henry supplies a test for revenge entertained in the heart: never say you will do a thing you cannot in faith pray to God to assist you in.
Henry explains the repetition of the proverb on weights by supposing the sin so common that men made light of it, pretending there was no trading without false weights.
Keil and Delitzsch note that the first line of the last verse is borrowed from a psalm where it carries a different sense, of gracious assistance rather than general disposal.
themes: A sin repeated because it was common
Steps a man does not command

25.pericope_label: It is a snare to the man who devoureth that which is holy, and after vows to make enquiry. A wise king scattereth the wicked, and bringeth the wheel over them. The spirit of man is the candle of the LORD, searching all the inward parts of the belly
debates: What the twenty-fifth verse means: Keil and Delitzsch and Ellicott read it of a man who cries holy in haste and looks into his vow only afterwards, while Henry, Clarke and Gill keep the received sense of sacrilege, of holy things turned to private use.

How dim the candle of the spirit is: Gill alone insists it was bright at first but through sin has become feeble, so that men only grope by it, while Henry, Clarke and Ellicott treat it as a sufficient inward guide.
outliers: Keil and Delitzsch and Clarke both rule out the punishment of the wheel, the one calling it only a terrible custom of war and the other denying that the threshing of subjects by kings is meant.
Henry extends devouring what is holy to those who hurry over their praying and preaching out of impatience to be done.
Clarke reports with discomfort that his own old English Bible renders the verse as though it were about vowing to saints.

Keil and Delitzsch observe that the word used names the self-conscious personal spirit as distinct from the spirit of a beast, and that the commoner word for the medium of bodily life is deliberately avoided.
themes: Vows made faster than they are weighed

28.pericope_label: Mercy and truth preserve the king: and his throne is upholden by mercy. The glory of young men is their strength: and the beauty of old men is the gray head. The blueness of a wound cleanseth away evil: so do stripes the inward parts of the belly
debates: What the blueness of a wound is: Clarke alone takes it for the scar formed when the two lips of a wound are joined in healing, while Ellicott renders it wounds that cut into the flesh and Keil and Delitzsch cannot settle the predicate at all.
outliers: Keil and Delitzsch say the pair of words guarding the king has no equivalent in their own language, and render it grace and truth of God, love and truth of men, kindness and truth of the divine forces.
Ellicott warns the old that if they do not receive the honour due to them the fault is their own, for not having spent their earlier years so as to make old age venerable.
Clarke observes that each age has its own vanity, the young affecting strength and agility and the old affecting wisdom and prudent counsel.

Clarke reports that six verses of this chapter are missing from two ancient versions and four others stand in a different place, and confesses he cannot account for it unless leaves were misplaced in the manuscripts.
themes: Each age with its own honour
